newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Israel, PLO to stay calm, resume talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Israel, PLO to stay calm, resume talks.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday criticised Israel for going ahead with a controversial housing project, voiced hopes that there would be no violent Palestinian reaction and urged both sides to resume talks.

"I think that the Israelis understand the difficulties that we see with their going forward," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said as Israeli bulldozers moved in to tear up a hillside for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Albright, briefing reporters before a U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki this week, noted President Bill Clinton had said publicly that he wished Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had not decided to start the project.

Israel claims the right to build anywhere in Jerusalem, which it calls its undivided capital. But Palestinians say the project tampers with the demographic balance before a final agreement on the status of the city.
Asked about a possible violent Palestinian backlash, Albright said: "We are obviously concerned about the fact that violence is never an answer to the problems in the Middle East.

"We would very much want to see a return to the (negotiating) table," she said. "That is the only time that there has been progress in the Middle East...when the parties are actually talking to each other at the table. And that is the way we would like to see things proceed."
Albright declined further comment and her cautiously worded remarks reflected the sensitive U.S. position as mediator between the Israelis and Palestinians.

"We are calling on all sides, and extremists on both sides, Israel and Palestinian, to refrain from violence because that's the language of the past," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said later.
The two sides needed to set a date for "final status" talks on the future of Palestinian self-rule areas that were supposed to have started Monday, Burns told a news briefing.

"It may take a lot of work to get them now to do that, and the United States will be in the thick of the action in suggesting that they get together informally to arrange those final status talks," he said.
"We're in a very difficult period in the peace negotiations. It's a period that's quite troubled, with animosity and distrust on both sides," he added.
Burns dismissed claims by Netanyahu Tuesday that the Palestinian leadership had given a "green light" to guerrilla groups to go ahead with bus bombings and suicide attacks.

"We have not seen any evidence that Chairman Arafat has given the green light to anybody to incite violence in Jerusalem or the West Bank or the Gaza Strip. On the contrary we have recent assurances from Chairman Arafat that he stands against violence," Burns said.

"I know there have been some statements by Israeli leaders today that there's been a green light given. We don't believe it to be true and we certainly will expect that Chairman Arafat keeps his commitment to Israel and to the United States that there be no violence."
U.S. officials say Netanyahu ignored appeals last week by both Clinton and Albright not to proceed with the housing project on a hill known to Arabs as Jabal Abu Ghneim and to Israelis as Har Homa.
Burns said Albright had not been in touch with the Israelis or Palestinians in the past two days but that Middle East envoy Dennis Ross had been talking to both sides.
